variants.headline: A bargain with {{partner}}, and gold in the terms
body: Our envoys and {{partner}} have sealed a bargain, and gold sits among its clauses. The exchange is plain: we hand over {{weGive}}, and {{weGet}} comes back to us. In the market square, a money-changer who has heard too many promises says he will weigh the coin himself when it arrives.

variants.headline: The terms of the bargain
body: Outgoing: {{weGive}}.
Incoming: {{weGet}}.
The gold entry is inked and witnessed, with a blank line left beneath it for the next reckoning.

variants.headline: Hear it! Terms are struck with {{partner}}
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}, hear it! {{partner}} has agreed, and gold is in the bargain! We hand over {{weGive}}; {{weGet}} returns to us! Watch the bread stalls, for prices move before the coin does!

variants.headline: The envoys earn their keep
body: Read the terms for yourself, {{terms.civic.people}}: {{partner}} has set a seal to the page, we give {{weGive}}, we gain {{weGet}}, and gold settles the balance. Such a bargain does not fall from the sky. Your {{terms.civic.government}} kept its envoys at the table until the last clause was agreed, and every workshop with an order to fill will feel the result before the quarter closes.

variants.headline: A trade route bound for us is plundered
body: A caravan carrying goods for our market was set upon before it reached the gate, and its load is gone. In the cloth rows, a draper has moved three bolts to the back shelf and told her regulars the price holds only until the shelf is bare. What the road loses, the counter pays for.

variants.headline: {{plunderer}} robs the road to our gates
body: {{plunderer}}'s raiders fell on a caravan bound for our gates and carried off the load. They struck where the road dips out of sight of the gate, a spot any patient band would choose. A captain who rides that stretch says the next caravan should not travel it without spears.

variants.headline: Payday for the raiders
body: The raiders who hit a caravan bound for us rode off with {{gold}} gold. At the unloading yard, a porter turned his slate face down and told the foreman he would not stand the gate road after dark for the same copper. His neighbor has begun sending her children to the well in pairs.

variants.headline: Trade needs a guarded road
body: A caravan meant for our merchants was emptied on the road, and the shippers are asking what the {{terms.civic.government}} intends for the next one. The answer so far is that guarding a road is expensive, as though the cost of losing the goods were nothing. Either put armed men beside the bales or tell the merchant plainly that the road is his own risk.

variants.headline: The road from {{origin}} is robbed
body: Word came up the road that the caravan from {{origin}} never arrived. Thieves met it at dusk, they say, and the drivers walked home with empty carts and a story they will tell all winter. Our market grows thin at the edges, the merchants in {{origin}} grow quiet, and somewhere a band is drinking to a fine week.

variants.headline: Our outgoing trade has stopped
body: The last road our merchants used for trade beyond our borders has closed, and no caravan of ours sets out on it now. Bales packed for foreign buyers sit under sheeting in the warehouses. At the depot, the loading master has hung his tally board on a nail and given his crew leave to look for other work.

variants.headline: The weights are put away
body: The road to the foreign market served our merchants well while it lasted, and this season it stands idle. In its best years it carried our goods out and foreign coin back, and the yard that provisioned it worked by lamplight. The keeper of the scales has wrapped the weights in oilcloth and shut the chest.

variants.headline: Small exporters have less room to wait
body: At the last count {{routes}} roads of ours ran to foreign markets; this week the number is none. A merchant with goods already crated has nowhere to send them, and the workshop that cannot store a season of work will be first to let a hand go. Whoever let the final road close owes those shops an account of the cause and a date when another opens.

variants.headline: Notice to those who send trade out
body: Notice to shippers and warehouse keepers: no road of ours now runs to a foreign market. Store finished goods dry and counted, and take no new orders until a route is announced. The workshops continue; the warehouses hold.

variants.headline: Trade run complete between cities {{routeDistance}} apart
body: A caravan has finished the run between {{ourCity}} and {{theirCity}}, a road of {{routeDistance}}. The bales came off the carts gray with dust, and the customs clerk logged every one before he would let the drivers eat. He says the merchants are already asking about a second run before the weather changes.

variants.headline: The next order from {{theirCity}}
body: Our traders have taken a full load from {{ourCity}} to {{theirCity}} and come home with the road behind them. The prize is not the single cargo but the custom a second run would fix: a buyer in {{theirCity}} who learns our measures will ask for them again. A workshop in {{ourCity}} that can fill such an order twice will have its next season spoken for.

variants.headline: A long road ends at {{ourCity}}
body: Word reaches the printing house that a caravan from {{theirCity}} has finished the road to {{ourCity}}, all {{routeDistance}} of it. The driver spent his first evening at the gate yard brushing dust from his team while a boy from the inn carried out water. A town that treats such a visitor well will see his wheels again next season.

variants.headline: A trade run with {{partner}} enters the record
body: The entry for this season records a completed run between {{theirCity}} and {{ourCity}}, a road of {{routeDistance}}, with {{partner}} written in the margin. The scribe set down the goods by kind and count, then the names of the merchants who pledged for them. He left the page open at the bottom, as is done when a road is expected to be used again.

variants.headline: A run of {{routeDistance}}, completed
body: Full run done: {{ourCity}} and {{theirCity}}, {{routeDistance}}. Nothing lost on the road. Buyers are already asking about the next one.

variants.headline: Raiders cut short an outgoing trade route
body: One of our outbound caravans has been stripped on the road, and its cargo will never reach a buyer. The dispatch yard spent the morning returning fees to merchants who had paid for space, and the clerk marked each name with a small cross. Nothing on that road has grown safer for the next load.

variants.headline: {{plunderer}} takes our trade on the road
body: {{plunderer}} took one of our caravans apart on the road and kept the goods. The drivers walked back with empty hands and a full story. The carters and the stallkeepers will feel this week's loss; the men who signed the papers will feel none of it.

variants.headline: The account of a plundered route
body: Caravans lost: one, and it left from our own soil.
Gold taken by the raiders: {{gold}}.
Cargo: gone. The loss is entered beside the road that closed.

variants.headline: Trade route to {{destination}} plundered
body: A caravan of ours headed for {{destination}} has been robbed on the road. In the dispatch yard this evening, a merchant is folding a letter to the buyers who were promised the load. "Tell them plainly," she says. "A late cart is better than a rumor."

variants.headline: Send the spears with the trade
body: Another of our caravans is gone, {{terms.civic.people}}, and the robbers are already counting the profit. A thief weighs the purse against the guard, and on our roads the guard is a rumor. Put spears beside the bales and robbery will cost more than it pays.

variants.headline: Our trade goes abroad
body: Carts loaded for foreign markets rolled out of the gate this week, and the last count had found no road at all. Our roads abroad now number {{routes}}. At the north gate warehouse, the keeper has lifted the bar from a door that had stayed shut and swept the threshold twice for good measure.

variants.headline: Hear it! Our trade goes abroad
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! Our goods go out to foreign markets! The roads abroad now number {{routes}}, and at the last count we had none! Every cart that leaves carries our mark, and every cart that comes home carries our pay!

variants.headline: What a new market can do for one kiln
body: The new roads abroad number {{routes}}, and the useful question is what they change for a single workshop at home. A potter who fires one order a month must still heat the kiln through, and a second buyer on the same firing pays for the heat twice over. The {{terms.civic.government}} has opened the way; the potters must make the ware worth the journey.

variants.headline: The road out stands open
body: A road with no cart is only a long walk. Ours comes home heavy.

variants.headline: We plunder a foreign trade route
body: A foreign caravan met our soldiers on the road and did not continue its journey. The wagons came back to our depot, where a quartermaster is now weighing sacks that still carry another ruler's seal. The load will feed the stores or fill the market, and the merchants who sent it will hear only that the road swallowed their goods.

variants.headline: {{gold}} gold taken from a foreign route
body: Our soldiers took {{gold}} gold from a foreign caravan along with its cargo. At the pay table, a clerk is weighing coin stamped with another sovereign's face and setting it in a separate pile. The sum will help balance this month's books; the merchants who lost it will remember the road and the men who held it.

variants.headline: A route from {{origin}} to {{destination}} is plundered
body: Letters from the frontier relate that a caravan bound from {{origin}} to {{destination}} was stopped by our soldiers and brought in with its goods. That the cargo will sell we do not doubt, nor that the officers will hear praise for it. We observe only that a great power takes what it intends to keep, while a highwayman takes whatever the road offers.

variants.headline: Foreign trade turns a profit
body: Merchants wait years for a foreign market to pay. A soldier with a good road can collect the same profit before supper.

variants.headline: Have we no merchants left?
body: Sir, I have spent my working life on roads like the one our soldiers just closed, and I know the families at both ends. The loss is not only the goods in the wagon but the handshake that sent it out. When we want that road again, the men at the far end will remember whose flag stopped their carts.
